structured_output.summary: I searched for public CIFAR-100 speedrun records, newer CIFAR-10 speedrun tricks, Muon variants, accuracy levers that cost no time, and hardware guidance on what makes conv layers cheap. There is no public CIFAR-100 recipe to copy. The AIDDA repo has no PRs, only the 59.3 s organizer baseline. The futurebiohackers PR (8.11 s), which several hypotheses cite, now returns 404. The tip at ~4.46 s is far ahead of anything public. The most actionable new directions: (1) Several augmented copies per image at equal compute. Fort et al. 2021 report CIFAR-100 gains at large batch without retuning the LR, saturating at ~4 copies. This is a new structural accuracy lever, though their training ran far longer than ~7 epochs. (2) Group-3 width set by tile alignment. 576 = 4.5x128, so 640 may cost almost nothing extra and 512 may save more than its FLOPs (NVIDIA guidance; consistent with E080). Profile it, no scored run first. (3) Fixes to the depth-cut design for H2.18.1. In airbench96, conv2/conv3 form a residual branch, so 'remove conv3' needs a choice about the skip. Group 2's conv3, the largest target (~14% of conv work by my count from the tree's shapes), is not in H2.18.1's probe. airbench95 (2 convs, no residual) does about half the per-epoch FLOPs of airbench96, but the paper gives no isolated ablation. External evidence lowers the prior on momentum schedules (CIFAR-100 -1.7 pp), cheaper or adaptive Muon variants (tested only on LLMs; MUD is weaker per step), and the hiverge, Fable and auto-research tricks (already tested, forbidden, or covered). Coarse-label auxiliary loss is new to the tree, but no paper I found quantifies it at short budgets, and it may break the rules.

findings.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.13343 (Fort et al. 2021, 'Drawing Multiple Augmentation Samples Per Image During Training Efficiently Decreases Test Error'); details via https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2105.13343
findings.claim: Drawing several augmented samples of the same image in one minibatch raises test accuracy for both small- and large-batch training. 'Crucially, this benefit arises even if different numbers of augmentations per image perform the same number of parameter updates and gradient evaluations (requiring the same total compute).' On CIFAR-100 (WRN-16-4) the benefit saturates at a multiplicity of about 4. At large batch, higher multiplicity wins without changing the optimal LR; at small batch it needs a smaller LR. The authors argue that variance from data augmentation harms generalization.
findings.relevance: This is a structural accuracy lever at zero time cost, which H6/H9 say is what's missing (all scalar knobs are null). The time stays the same because the batch size and the number of forward/backward passes do not change. The risk: the paper's regime is long training, and at ~7 epochs, halving the number of unique images per epoch could cost data coverage. The safest test is multiplicity 2, only in the 32 px phase (bs 1024 = 512 unique images x 2 independent flip/translate draws), so samples per step and the step count stay unchanged. Check how this interacts with the alternating-flip scheme.

findings.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.09335 (Hoffer et al., Batch Augmentation, CVPR 2020)
findings.claim: Batch augmentation fills larger batches with augmented copies of the same images. It cuts the number of SGD updates needed (e.g., 94.15% in 23 epochs vs 93.07% at 100 epochs for the baseline), but the comparison is matched in steps, not compute, because each step does more work.
findings.relevance: This shows that the compute-matched version (Fort et al.) is the only form usable as a time lever here. The Hoffer form would raise per-step cost in the energy-bound 32 px phase.

findings.claim: Convolutions run as implicit GEMMs. Forward: M = N*P*Q, N = K (output channels), K = C*R*S. Data gradient: M = N*H*W, N = C. Weight gradient: M = C*R*S, N = K, K = N*P*Q. Tile quantization: if a dimension does not divide into the tile size, the padded part of each tile is computed and wasted. Wave quantization: the A100 has 108 SMs, so tile counts just above a multiple of 108 add a whole extra wave. NVIDIA recommends channel counts divisible by 64 or, ideally, 256.
findings.relevance: Group 3's width of 576 is 4.5 x 128. If cuDNN uses 128-wide N tiles, 576 already pays for 640 in every group-3 GEMM. An untested capacity lever follows: widening group 3 to 640 may be close to time-free, costing only ~11% more group-3 elementwise work, which is small at 7x7/3x3 maps. Conversely, 512 might recover more than its FLOP share, unlike E080's group-2 cuts. Example: at bs 1024 and 32 px, group-3 conv2/3 have M = 1024*9 = 9216 = 72 tiles of 128, and N = 576 gives 5 tiles, 360 tiles in total (3.33 waves of 108). 640 also gives 360 tiles, and 512 gives 288 (2.67 waves). If the logged kernel names show 64-wide tiles, 576 = 9x64 has no waste and the idea is dead. Decide from the existing per-(layer, shape) kernel names (E094/E099 logs) before any scored run. The same arithmetic matters for H2.11.5: bs 768 at 32 px gives M = 6912 = 54 tiles, i.e. 2.5 waves, so per-step efficiency changes.

findings.claim: Each airbench96 ConvGroup is conv1 -> MaxPool2d(2) -> BN -> GELU, then a residual branch conv2 -> BN -> GELU -> conv3 -> BN, added to the post-pool activation x0, then GELU. CIFAR-10 widths are 128/384/512. conv1 runs before the pool, at the pre-pool resolution.
findings.relevance: This affects the design of H2.18.1. In this lineage, conv2 and conv3 together form the residual branch, so 'remove conv3' is ambiguous. Keeping a 1-conv residual branch is a different net from airbench94/95's 2 convs with no residual. The probe should define the variant: either drop the whole residual branch (conv2 + conv3) or keep a single conv plus the skip. From the tree's own shapes (32 px, 31->15->7->3 maps; conv MACs per image ≈ g1 conv1 27M, g1 conv2/3 33M each, g2 conv1 100M, g2 conv2/3 65M each, g3 conv1 98M, g3 conv2/3 27M each), removing group 2's conv3 is the largest single depth cut (~14% of conv MACs). Group 1's conv3 (~7%) and group 3's conv3 (~6%) save less. H2.18.1 currently probes only the group-1 and group-3 conv3. Group 1's pre-pool 31x31x128 activation is the largest memory-traffic site for the ~30% elementwise share.

findings.claim: airbench95 keeps 2 convs per block with no residual, widths 128/384/384, 15 epochs, and uses 1.4e15 total FLOPs for 95%. airbench96 adds a third conv per block plus a residual across the later two convs, widths 128/512/512, 12 px Cutout, 40 epochs, 7.2e15 FLOPs for 96%. The paper has no isolated ablation of the third conv or the residual, and it notes diminishing accuracy returns per FLOP for the airbench96 architecture.
findings.relevance: This gives a weak external prior for H2.18. Per epoch, airbench95's net costs ~9.3e13 FLOPs against airbench96's ~1.8e14 (about half, though the widths also differ). It is the only public evidence on depth vs accuracy in this family, and it does not separate depth from width or epochs. Treat depth cuts as unproven, consistent with H2.18's low prior.

findings.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28921 (Critical Damping as a Momentum Schedule)
findings.claim: The momentum schedule mu(t) = 1 - 2*sqrt(alpha(t)) reaches 90% on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 2.34x faster but ends -0.46 pp lower. On CIFAR-100 'the accuracy cost grows (-1.7 pp), compressing the accuracy-matched gain to 1.14x'.
findings.relevance: External evidence against a momentum-schedule lever on CIFAR-100. It agrees with E027 (Muon momentum 0.85: -1.18 pp) and the flat 0.5-0.6 optimum, and supports keeping Muon momentum closed under H7.1.

findings.claim: MUD 'typically converges slightly slower per step than Muon but with substantially lower optimizer overhead', with wall-clock gains on GPT-2 large and ESM-2 only. NorMuon adds per-neuron second-moment row normalization after orthogonalization (+11.3% efficiency over Muon at 1.1B LLM pretraining). Neither paper reports vision, CNN or CIFAR experiments.
findings.relevance: Low prior for this tree. Per-step quality is binding here (E031: 2 NS steps cost -1.8 pp), so MUD's weaker steps would likely cost more than its saving. NorMuon's per-row normalization overlaps with the filter renorm plus BN already in place, and it is untested on CNNs. Supports keeping cheaper orthogonalizers closed (H7.2).

findings.claim: The official CIFAR-100 speedrun repo has 0 pull requests (open or closed) and lists only the organizer's ResNet9-style baseline (75.36%, 59.30 s). The forks checked (RyanChong0117, Daniel-T-S-Adams) contain no submissions. The best public result is the futurebiohackers PR (75.29% in 8.11 s on an A100), and that page now returns 404.
findings.relevance: There is no external CIFAR-100 recipe faster than the tip to borrow from: the loop's ~4.46-4.70 s is about 1.7x faster than the best public result. Several hypotheses' sources (the futurebiohackers PR) can no longer be checked online.

findings.claim: hiverge's 1.98 s CIFAR-10 changes: a vectorized/batched Muon with periodic renorm, vectorized cropping, brightness/contrast augmentation, a compiled forward+backward, GELU->SiLU, SVD-based whitening init, fp16 + channels_last, selective (confidence-gated) TTA, and hyperparameter tuning. No ablation numbers are published.
findings.relevance: Nothing new for the tree. SiLU was refuted (E003). Brightness/contrast was refuted only under SGD at 8 epochs (E008) and never retested under Muon, but its prior is low. SVD whitening is math-equivalent. Any TTA is forbidden by the rules. Batched Muon and renorm are already in the tip.

findings.claim: Fable's legitimate CIFAR-10 gain (1.98 -> 1.828 s, 7.6%) came from progressive resizing (24 -> 28 -> full res), pooling improvements, and CUDA-graph/optimizer-fusion work. The gains removed in regrading came from moving augmentation into untimed setup (~16 ms), choosing faster hosts, and an untimed 60 s GPU cooldown (~9 ms).
findings.relevance: Confirms that the tree already covers all of Fable's legitimate levers (H2.1, H2.14). The disallowed items (precomputed augmentation, thermal cooldown) match bans in this task's rules, so none are usable.

findings.claim: On CIFAR-10 airbench96, agents cut wall-clock time 4.59% (26.36 -> 25.15 s) by removing validation overhead, shortening the schedule, raising the LR, and adding a faster warmup to recover the accuracy lost from the speedups.
findings.relevance: Nothing transfers. The warmup line is closed here (E051, E059), and the schedule trims are already at their exchange-rate limit (H2.10).

findings.claim: Each CIFAR-100 training image has a fine label and one of 20 coarse superclass labels. Hierarchy-aware losses (HCOT and others) are reported to improve CIFAR-100 classification, but no source I found quantifies fine-label gains for short training budgets.
findings.relevance: This direction is new to the tree: an auxiliary 20-way coarse head (576->20) or a hierarchy-aware smoothing term, at about zero time cost. Two caveats: no short-budget evidence was found, and RULES.md and the benchmark's data loader must be checked to see whether coarse labels are exposed and allowed (they come from the same training files, but the rules may restrict training to the provided fine labels). Low priority unless the rules clearly allow it.
